resources.string: Plug an ELM327 adapter into the OBD-II port (usually under the steering column) and switch the ignition on. The engine does not have to run, but RPM, air flow and temperatures only appear once it does.

Pair the adapter in the phone\'s Bluetooth settings first (the usual PIN is 1234 or 0000). Only paired devices are listed: scanning for new ones would require location access, which diagnostics does not need.
Wi-Fi adapters create their own network — join it in the phone settings. The usual address is 192.168.0.10, port 35000.
A virtual car inside the app: every screen works without an adapter or a vehicle. The data is plausible but not real.
Bluetooth is off or unsupported on this device
No paired devices. Pair the adapter in Bluetooth settings and come back.
Android 12 and newer require a separate permission before the app can talk to paired devices.
Lost the adapter: it was unplugged, the ignition went off, or the bus went quiet.

This is the pause between cycles: parameters refresh once per exchange-plus-pause. One exchange costs 25-60 ms, and there are more parameters than fit in a single request - that is where the whole cycle comes from. Zero means no pause. Cheap adapters start losing answers with no pause: if values freeze, increase it.
Send a command straight to the adapter: ATI for the version, ATRV for voltage, 010C for RPM. The reply is shown as is.
No adapter connected. Open the Link tab and connect — or switch on demo mode to see the app without a car.
What to show on the gauges

OBD-II has no gear parameter - the app works it out from rpm and speed. On a manual that works even better than on an automatic, but the car has to be moving: standing still there is nothing to compute from.
Fuel left in the tank divided by consumption.
This car does not report the fuel level, so there is nothing to compute the range from and the tile is hidden.
not listed by the car - may not answer
The list holds only what this car reports. The remaining standard parameters are not supported by it.

This engine has neither an air-flow meter nor a ready fuel-rate PID, so the app works it out from manifold pressure, rpm and temperature. It is an estimate: compare it against a fill-up and adjust Volumetric efficiency on the Vehicle tab.
Nothing to work consumption out from: the car did not report %1$s. The app uses a ready fuel rate, an air-flow meter or manifold pressure - with none of those there is nowhere to get it.
The average and the litres come from the trip recording - start it on the Measurements tab. The instant figure works without recording.
No faults: the ECU has not stored a single code.
Could not read the codes: the ECU did not answer. That does not mean there are none - check that the ignition is on and try again.

Mismatch: the lamp status reports %1$d stored codes, but the request returned %2$d. This happens when the counter in the ECU also counts codes that do not light the lamp, or when another module holds them. The raw answer is visible in the adapter terminal on the Connection screen: command 03.
Saved automatically after every read and visible without the car - so the codes can be worked through at home instead of in the garage. The last ten reads are kept.
Empty so far. After the first read the entries appear here and stay, even once the adapter is unplugged.
The ECU saw the fault once and is waiting to see whether it repeats — the lamp is not on yet.
These cannot be cleared by hand: the ECU clears them itself after several clean drive cycles.
Manufacturer-specific code: the exact meaning depends on the make.

Clearing turns the Check Engine lamp off and erases the stored codes together with the freeze frame, but it does not fix the cause: if the fault is still there, the code returns within a drive or two.\n\nIt also resets the readiness monitors — the car will fail an emissions test until the ECU has run them again.
The ECU refused the clear command
What the engine was doing when the ECU stored the fault.

The Read codes button above asks the engine only - that is what OBD-II covers. An ABS or airbag lamp has its code in its own module, at its own address on the same bus. Manufacturers do not publish those addresses, so the app walks the whole diagnostic range and sees who answers. Takes about half a minute. Read-only: clearing another module is not offered here and will not be.
No module answered. Either nothing but the engine is on this bus, or the modules only talk to the manufacturer tool.
Module discovery only works on 11-bit CAN. This car uses a different protocol where module addressing works differently, and the app will not send commands blindly.
This address is inside the OBD-II range - most likely the engine or transmission, whose codes the normal read above already shows.
The module is there but would not hand over the codes: %1$s. Usually that means a manufacturer tool with a security key is required.
Failure type: %1$02X (open circuit, short or out of range - the exact meaning is the manufacturer\'s).
All monitors complete — ready for an emissions test
This car does not report a VIN: service 09 is not supported by every ECU.
Taken from the 10th VIN character. The year code repeats every 30 years, so cars from the 1980s may be off by one cycle.
VIN check digit does not match — the VIN was read incorrectly
This VIN carries no check digit (it is mandatory for North America only)
Recording has not started. Data is logged while the app is connected to the adapter.

Distance and fuel come from the car itself — speed and air flow, no GPS. Fuel from air flow is an estimate: on a cold engine and at full throttle the ECU enriches the mixture, so real consumption is higher.
The file is ready. On Android 9 writing to the Downloads folder would need an extra permission — send the CSV to yourself with Share.

BLE adapters (Bluetooth 4.0 and newer) usually are not paired in advance and do not show up in the paired list - scanning finds them. A classic ELM327, in contrast, has to be paired once in the phone settings.
This phone has no Bluetooth Low Energy
On Android 8–11 the system cannot scan for BLE devices without precise location access: Bluetooth beacons can reveal where you are. The app does not need, read or send your location.
If the link drops (ignition off, you walked away), the app retries on its own - up to three times.
Larger means more scrolling, but it reads from the driver seat without leaning in. Gauge numbers shrink to fit their tile instead of being cut off.
Gears are learned while driving: %1$d so far
Acceleration and braking are measured automatically from vehicle data. Bus speed arrives as whole km/h a few times per second - enough to compare your own runs, not to argue with the brochure.
Come to a stop and pull away - the run starts by itself.
Power is derived from mass, acceleration and drag. Road gradient and wind are ignored and mass comes from the profile - so this is an estimate for comparing runs, not a dyno figure.
Range, power estimate and gauge scales depend on these numbers - the OBD-II bus does not report them. Set them once for your car.
Only used to work out consumption on engines without an air-flow meter. 80 is mid-range for a naturally aspirated engine. If a fill-up shows the app read low, raise it; if it read high, lower it.
Does not look like a tyre size - expected 245/70R16

Manufacturers add their own parameters in service 22 - gearbox oil temperature, for instance. If you know the number and formula for your car, enter them and the parameter appears on the gauges. Service 01 is standard parameters, 22 is extended.
In a formula A, B, C… are the reply bytes in order; + - * / and brackets are available. Example: (A*256+B)/4
Check the fields - the formula or PID number could not be parsed

You do not need to turn mobile data off: the app binds the connection to the adapter network. If the phone leaves that network on its own (\"no internet access\"), tell it not to in the Wi-Fi settings for this network.
Connection bound to the adapter network
Could not bind the connection to the adapter network. If no data arrives, switch mobile data off while diagnosing.

Auto-detect always works, but cheap adapters redo the search on every connection. A 2016+ Patriot uses CAN 11 bit / 500 kbit/s — naming it directly saves a few seconds. If it turns out wrong, the app falls back to auto-detect.
Type what the repair manual for your car says. This text replaces the built-in one and survives a restart.
A description table from a file: one code per line, separated by a tab or a semicolon. An Excel export and a windows-1251 file both work.
No codes found in that file. It needs to be a text file with one code per line: P1513\tdescription
Voltage at the OBD-II connector (adapter) — practically the voltage at the battery.
ECU supply voltage (PID 42) — the adapter did not report its own. It reads slightly lower than at the terminals.
From the resting voltage. A fair reading comes 15–20 minutes after stopping: right after a drive the surface charge makes the battery look better than it is.

Before chasing a fault: the adapter measures at its own connector, not at the terminals, and reads low. Measure at the terminals with the engine running - if it is 13.8-14.4 V the alternator is fine, and the difference goes into Voltage correction below.

Press this, then turn the key. The app switches to fast voltage-only polling and catches the dip — the normal poll misses it, cranking lasts under a second. This is the main battery health test: below 9.6 V the battery is weak or the terminals are corroded.
Waiting for the start — turn the key
Why there is no current reading

Current cannot be read over OBD-II: SAE J1979 has no current parameter at all — not draw, not charge, not leakage. The engine ECU does not measure it, and neither does ELM327: the adapter only reports voltage.

Deriving it from voltage does not work either. The whole resting range of a battery is about 0.8 V across its full charge, so one percent is about 0.008 V. A 50 mA draw takes roughly 0.0005 V per hour out of a 75 Ah battery; even a 3 A draw is about 0.03 V. The adapter resolves 0.1 V — far coarser.

Leakage is found with a clamp meter or a multimeter in series with the negative terminal. The app cannot replace that and will not pretend to.

ELM327 clones are off by a tenth or two of a volt, and the difference between \"charged\" and \"low\" is exactly tenths. Measure at the terminals with a multimeter and enter the difference: if the adapter shows 12.4 and the multimeter 12.6, enter 0.2. Limit ±1 V.
No list of these numbers for ME17.9.7x exists in the open, but the ECU answers honestly: a refusal for a number that does not exist, a value for one that does. The sweep only reads, it never writes.
Numbers are hexadecimal, for example F400 and F4FF
The ECU answered nothing in this range. Try another one.

This is how you find a parameter that is in no documentation. Take a snapshot, switch on the headlights, the rear defogger and the blower at full, then press Compare. The parameter that moved with the load is the one you want.
What each one means, nobody can say without documentation. Press Use to add the number as your own parameter and work out the formula.

The app cannot measure current; it is measured with a clamp meter or a multimeter in series with the negative terminal. What the app can do is the arithmetic. Capacity comes from the profile: %1$.0f Ah — correct it on the Vehicle tab if yours differs.
Down to 50%% charge, below which a cold start may fail. Counted from the current %1$d%%, with no allowance for cold or self-discharge — in frost it will be less.
Of that, %1$d ms is the exchange with the adapter and the rest is the pause set above. With no pause it would be about %2$.1f per second.
The pause is off - all of this time is the exchange with the adapter, and it will not answer any faster.

That is the rate for rpm, speed and throttle. Temperature, fuel level and voltage are read on a full round every %1$d ms - they do not change in that time anyway, and the needle keeps up with the pedal.
Parameters are requested in one batch — all in a single exchange with the adapter. This is the fastest mode.
This adapter or ECU does not support batched requests, so parameters are read one by one and the cycle is that many times longer.
Not connected — connect on the \"Link\" tab. Demo mode works too: the virtual vehicle answers these services exactly like a real one.

Reads everything that can be read and puts it into one report: protocol and adapter, VIN, calibration ID and its verification number, MIL and trouble codes from all three services, monitor readiness, freeze frame, on-board test results and their performance counters. Nothing is written to the ECU. The report is saved as a PDF you can hand to a garage, attach to a sale listing or print. A text version is there too, for pasting the report straight into a message.
This is the slow part: one request per monitor, and a vehicle with two banks can have more than twenty. Without it the check takes seconds.
Report saved inside the app — send it with \"Share\"

This is the only place that shows the state of a component BEFORE the check engine light comes on. Mode 01 says \"the sensor is alive\", mode 03 says \"the sensor is already dead\", and here you get the number and the limits the ECU compares it against: how close the result came to the threshold. This is how you watch a catalyst that still passes, or an oxygen sensor that has started to get lazy.
Reading stopped — showing what was read.
The ECU returned no results. That happens: mode 06 is optional, and some vehicles (especially pre-2008) do not support it or return nothing until the monitors have run.

The bus reports their location in a single byte — but in two different layouts (PID 13 and 1D), and a vehicle supports exactly one. The app uses the one the vehicle declared: the same byte means different sensors in each layout.
Separate oxygen sensor tests (mode 05) do not exist on CAN — that is the standard: mode 06 carries the same data there. Mode 05 remains the only way to see sensor switch times on pre-2008 vehicles.

For each monitor the ECU keeps two numbers: how many times the test completed, and how many times the conditions for it occurred. Why it matters: after clearing codes, readiness reports \"complete\" after a single good cycle and the vehicle passes inspection. These counters show how many cycles the test actually ran — they tell a healthy system from a freshly cleared one.
The ECU did not return performance counters. They are not mandatory for every vehicle: older ones have none at all.
Both numbers count from the moment the counters were reset — clearing codes or disconnecting the battery does that.

Half of the complaints about diagnostic apps are complaints about the adapter: a clone answers \"ELM327 v2.1\", does not understand half of the commands and cheerfully answers \"OK\" to things it never does. The check does not ask the adapter who it is — it tries the commands the app\'s features rely on.

Looks like a clone: ELM327 versions 1.5 and 2.3 were never released, they are printed to look newer than the original. That is an indication, not proof, and by itself it does not matter — what matters is which commands below are supported.
Commands the adapter did not understand mean switched-off features, not a fault: the app works without them, but says so plainly instead of showing empty screens.
Scanning for non-OBD-II modules will not work with this adapter: it needs a custom request header and a receive filter, and the adapter did not understand them.

Clones misreport themselves to the Bluetooth stack in different ways: one does not publish an SPP service record and only opens by raw channel number, another rejects a secure socket, a third cannot do an insecure one. Trying them in turn finds a working method, but costs seconds on every connect — the one that worked can be pinned.
The adapter rejected the calibration — it does not support it

CALID is the calibration number the manufacturer changes with every official reflash, CVN is its checksum. A factory ID with a checksum that does not match means the firmware was modified — this is exactly how chip tuning is found at inspection. There is nothing to compare against (no open database of factory checksums exists), but the app lets you record yours now and compare after a garage visit.
What the ECU recorded and what it checks itself
The check engine light has not been read yet — connect and open \"Gauges\" or read the codes.
Check engine light on, codes in the ECU: %1$d
Monitors are complete — no questions on that part at inspection.
Monitors not complete: %1$d. Normal after clearing codes, but too early for inspection.
Read everything into one report with a single tap
How close a component is to its limit
Where they are and what their tests say
How many times a monitor actually ran
Tiles follow your finger: press and hold one to drag it onto a neighbour, or tap it to choose its width. Order and sizes are saved.
Too small to read? Press and hold a line — a magnifier appears. Drag it around without lifting your finger.
Pro is open to everyone for now: sales are not set up. You are seeing the app as someone without Pro would see it - the switch is on the Connection tab.
The app will show itself as a person without Pro sees it: paid sections stay where they are, but marked. Useful to see what is actually being sold.
The full check queries the whole car and puts the answers into one report - save it as PDF, send it to a workshop or attach it to a sale listing.
Module scan finds what OBD-II does not cover: ABS, airbags, transmission, power steering. The ABS light is on, yet ordinary apps report "no faults" - because they only look at the engine.
Custom parameters: your own formula over the module answer, a mode 22 sweep and a before/after snapshot - you can see which parameter moves when you press the pedal.
Trip recording: distance, average and top speed, idle time, fuel used and average consumption - with CSV export.
Acceleration and braking runs, power and torque estimated from acceleration - without a track or a dyno.
In-use performance counters show how many times the on-board tests have completed. They tell a healthy car from one whose codes were cleared right before the sale.
The cranking test shows the voltage drop while the starter turns, a voltage chart and a parasitic drain estimate - the thing that flattens a battery overnight.
A dashboard with no tile limit, with drag-to-reorder and per-tile size.
Fault archive: what was there last time and what changed.
%1$d tiles are shown for free. Remove the limit with Pro - or drop one tile to add another.
